about: Species that cannot reliably be told apart from a photo, or only from one particular view. WRITTEN BY CLAUDE FROM MEMORY on 13 November 2026. CHECK every line against a field guide or the recording scheme before relying on it. When the image model's top answer is in a group, Eira should say 'one of these' and give the reason, not pick one.

groups.why: Workers of the buff-tailed and white-tailed bumblebees cannot reliably be separated by eye. Queens and males usually can.
The ginger carder bees are very alike. Separating them needs a close view of the hairs on the sides of the thorax and on the abdomen, and worn bees often cannot be named.
The garden and ruderal bumblebees are very alike. Face length and band shape help but many photos will not show enough.
Black bumblebees with red tails: the red-tailed bumblebee, its cuckoo and the red-shanked carder bee. Wing colour and the hairs on the hind leg separate them.
These three are distinctive as fresh females, but most other mining bees (Andrena) need a microscope, so a mining bee that is not a clear match should be left at 'a mining bee'.
Common and German wasps are separated by the mark on the face and the pattern on the thorax, which a photo from above rarely shows.
Drone flies are separated by leg colour, the stripe on the face and the eye hairs. A photo needs to show the front legs and face.
Syrphus hoverflies cannot be separated from above. Females need a view of the hind leg, and males usually need a microscope.
These hoverflies differ in the shape of the yellow marks and whether they reach the edge of the abdomen. Many photos are not clear enough.
Platycheirus hoverflies are a large group of similar species. Males are named from their front legs, and many females cannot be named from a photo.
Only males with the long abdomen reaching past the wing tips can be named. Female Sphaerophoria cannot be separated from a photo.
Separated by the shape of the abdomen and its marks, which is hard to judge in a photo.
The common green lacewing is a group of species that cannot be separated by eye.
Black aphids on plants other than beans may be other species. Aphids are named from the plant they are on and often need a microscope.
Red ants (Myrmica) need a microscope to tell apart.
The whites are separated by the underside of the hindwing (green veins) and the size and shape of the black wing tip. A view from above alone is often not enough.
Small and Essex skippers are separated by the colour of the underside of the antenna tips, which needs a head-on photo.
Female common blues can be brown and look like the brown argus. The spots on the underside separate them.
The yellow underwings are variable. Size, the shape of the dark hindwing border and marks on the forewing separate them, and worn moths are hard.
Smoky and common wainscots are separated mainly by hindwing colour, which a resting moth hides.
The minors are small, variable moths. Several related species can only be named by dissection.
Vine's rustic, the uncertain and the rustic are very alike and often recorded together.
The spring quakers and the clouded drab are variable and overlap. Size and the shape of the marks help.
Footman moths are separated by wing shape and the yellow stripe along the front edge.
Grass moths are small and alike. Worn ones often cannot be named.
The small grey scopariine moths are hard to name from photos.
Most pugs are difficult. The lime-speck pug is distinctive, but many others are not safely named from a photo.
Common and ruddy darters are separated by leg colour (striped or all black) and the shape of the abdomen.
Azure and common blue damselflies are separated by the mark on the second segment and the stripes on the side of the thorax.
Grasshoppers vary a great deal in colour. They are named from the shape of the lines on the pronotum, wing length and song.
The oak bush-crickets are separated by wing length: the southern one has only tiny wing stubs.
The green shield bug and the southern green shield bug are alike, especially as nymphs.
Many black ground beetles look alike and need a close view of the legs and the shape of the thorax.
Several similar weevils occur in gardens.
False widow spiders are variable and overlap in pattern. Certain naming usually needs a specialist.
Banded snails are separated by the colour of the lip of the adult shell (dark or white), which must be in view, and a few break the rule.
Small brown garden snails are easily confused, especially when young.
Slugs vary and young ones differ from adults. Many slugs cannot be named from a photo, and some need dissection.
Female and young smooth and palmate newts are very alike. The throat (spotted or plain) separates them.
Common frogs have a dark patch behind the eye. Water frogs do not, and are harder to tell from one another.
Common and soprano pipistrelles are separated by the pitch of their calls on a bat detector, not by sight.
Wood mice and yellow-necked mice are separated by the yellow collar across the chest.
Field and bank voles differ in fur colour and tail length, which a quick photo may not show.
Chiffchaff and willow warbler are best told apart by song. Leg colour and wing length help in a good photo.
Marsh and willow tits are told apart most reliably by call.
Dandelions are a group of several hundred very similar microspecies. 'Dandelion' is as far as a photo goes.
Brambles are a group of several hundred microspecies. 'Bramble' is as far as a photo goes.
Wild roses hybridise and several look alike. Hips, sepals and prickles are needed.
